source_refs.note: Topic 8.6, printed pages 187-189: the structure of phloem and the pressure-flow theory. Figure 8.10 is carried by the xylem-phloem original shared with topic 8.5.

blocks.text: Phloem is the vascular tissue that transports organic nutrients, particularly the products of photosynthesis, from the leaves to the other parts of the plant where they are needed or stored. It generally lies on the outer side of both primary and secondary vascular tissue in plants with secondary growth, and it constitutes the inner bark. Phloem comprises sieve elements, companion cells, phloem fibres and phloem parenchyma.

blocks.alt: A longitudinal section of phloem. From left: narrow Phloem fibre cells; a column of Phloem Parenchyma cells with nuclei and vacuoles; a wide Sieve Tube Cell crossed by two Sieve Plates perforated by Sieve Pores; and narrow spindle-shaped Companion Cells, one with a nucleus, lying beside the sieve tube.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.10: Different components of phloem tissue (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.10).

blocks.text: The cells that transport sugars and other organic material are the sieve tube elements. They have sieve areas, parts of the cell wall where pores interconnect neighbouring elements; some sieve areas form in the end walls where the cells join end to end into a longitudinal series, the sieve tube. Each sieve tube element is associated with one or more companion cells, which communicate with it through plasmodesmata and supply it with ATP and proteins. Phloem parenchyma stores substances such as sugars, resins, latex and mucilage that are important for plant defence and moisture retention.

Sugars are transported through the phloem. Diffusion is far too slow to account for the speed of sugar movement in phloem, which averages 1 metre per hour, whereas diffusion would take eight years to cover 1 metre.

The pressure-flow theory, also called the mass-flow hypothesis, is the most widely accepted explanation of sugar transport in the phloem. Translocation moves sugar from the source, where it is synthesised, to the sink, where it is consumed or stored. Proposed by Ernst Munch in 1930, the theory rests on the difference in osmotic pressure between source and sink.

items: The glucose made by photosynthesis in the mesophyll cells is used in respiration; the excess is converted into the non-reducing sugar sucrose.

Sucrose is actively transported from the mesophyll cells into the companion cells of the phloem, and from there diffuses through plasmodesmata into the sieve tubes, so the concentration of sucrose in the sieve tubes rises.

Because of the higher sucrose (solute) concentration in the sieve tubes, water moves into them by osmosis from the nearby xylem of the leaf, raising the water potential at the source end of the sieve tubes.

At the sink end, sugar is actively unloaded from the sieve tubes and water follows by osmosis; the exit of water lowers the water potential at the sink end. So there is a higher water potential at the source end and a lower one at the sink end.
The difference in water potential makes water flow from source to sink, and since the sucrose is dissolved in the water it is carried along from source to sink.

blocks.alt: A xylem column on the left and a phloem sieve tube in the middle, with a leaf (source of sucrose) and its companion cell at the top right and a fruit (sink for sucrose) with its companion cell at the bottom right; plasmodesmata join the companion cells to the sieve tube.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.11: The pressure-flow theory (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.11).
blocks.long_description: A xylem column on the left and a phloem sieve tube in the middle, with a leaf (source of sucrose) and its companion cell at the top right and a fruit (sink for sucrose) with its companion cell at the bottom right; plasmodesmata join the companion cells to the sieve tube. Numbered steps: 1 sugar made in the leaf; 2 sucrose actively loaded into the companion cell and sieve tube; 3 water enters the sieve tube from the xylem by osmosis (higher hydrostatic pressure); 4 sucrose actively unloaded into the fruit and water follows (lower hydrostatic pressure); 5 bulk flow of solution down the sieve tube. Legend: water, sucrose, osmosis, active transport of sucrose.
